summary:
Penang stands under Malaysia's federal framework. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code criminalise 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' and acts of 'gross indecency', carrying up to 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping. The offences are not confined to Malaysian citizens, so a foreign visitor in Penang is exposed to them on the same terms as a resident. Sodomy has been criminalised in the territory since 1871.

Sharia enactments add a second, narrower layer. Every one of Malaysia's 13 states and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya criminalise cross-dressing or 'a man posing as a woman', with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning; three of them also bar women from posing as men. These offences reach Muslims only, so a non-Muslim visitor is not subject to them, and the enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing. Enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments.

Litigation has narrowed the state layer without loosening the federal one. A High Court declined to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional, and the Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving the Penal Code offences fully intact. A constitutional challenge was still pending as of late 2014, filed after religious officers and police arrested 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Enforcement against gender nonconformity is active and publicly authorised. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) had his 'full licence to carry out its enforcement actions' against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for 'insulting Islam' before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection.

The documented pattern of exposure is venue-based raid and public outing rather than individual stops. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B, the largest operation of its kind since 2022. Media were pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were published; 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended. A magistrate rejected a remand extension for lack of ground, yet release was delayed, with more than 130 people held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid; on 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna, this one in Penang.

Trans people in Malaysia also face lethal violence met with official indifference. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading 'The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself'.

The surrounding climate is one of state-backed restriction. Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects, government-funded mukhayyam 'rehabilitation' retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events and media content are censored. There is no same-sex marriage, no legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded for Malaysia, and no law prohibits discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor, the practical exposure in Penang is the Penal Code, not the Sharia enactments. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the risk concentrates in raids on venues where attendees are arrested and named.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch and Justice For Sisters published 'I Don't Want to Change Myself', on anti-LGBT conversion practices, discrimination and violence in Malaysia, on 10 August 2022. It draws on interviews with 73 LGBT people across Malaysia between 2018 and 2021, documents the federal penal code's punishment of oral and anal sex with up to 20 years in prison, and records that at least 1,733 people had attended government-run 'rehabilitation' programmes as of June 2021. Penang is among the states where interviewees lived, but the report documents national-level patterns and contains no Penang-specific enforcement case.

The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Malaysia, last updated 16 December 2025, states that no legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded and that discrimination and violence against LGBT people are regularly reported, with transgender people particularly vulnerable. Enforcement activity since the 2018 election includes an October 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur with at least 20 LGBT people arrested, an August raid on an LGBT venue in which twenty men were arrested, a Terengganu Sharia court ordering a lesbian couple caned, and November 2023 plans in Johor to establish conversion-therapy centres.

The direction of travel at state level has been restriction rather than decriminalisation, and the federal offences have survived every constitutional attack brought against the layers around them.
localsOnly:
Malaysians who are Muslim are subject to both the Penal Code and their state Sharia enactment, and can be prosecuted by state Islamic religious departments for cross-dressing as well as for same-sex intimacy. Residents therefore face a double exposure that a non-Muslim visitor does not.

Government-funded mukhayyam 'rehabilitation' retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and the state apparatus publicly backs enforcement: the July 2020 authorisation given to the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department was not withdrawn, and no legal gender-recognition procedure exists for residents seeking corrected documents.

Legal advocacy organisations such as Justice For Sisters have intervened directly in arrest cases, arranging bailors and legal aid, and their documentation records police mistreatment of trans women in custody as well as impunity for killings.

There is no anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, no same-sex marriage, and no partner recognition of any kind, so employment, housing and family claims offer residents no statutory footing.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Penang's own Sharia enactment bars women from posing as men is not sourced here; the inventory establishes only that three of the 13 states do.

No Penang-specific enforcement proceeding appears in the Human Rights Watch material, and the Penang sauna raid of early December 2025 is described in the sources without an arrest total, charges, or outcome.

The status of the constitutional challenge pending as of late 2014, filed after the mass arrest of 16 trans women on 8 June 2014, is unresolved in this inventory; no later judgment on it is recorded.

Whether a legal gender-recognition procedure exists in practice through court or administrative channels, as distinct from statute, is not stated by the sources, which record only that none is on the books.

The disposition of the men arrested in the 28 November 2025 Chow Kit operation, and whether the Home Minister's 2 December remarks produced any change to section 377B, remain unverified.
